title: Seven Woes and a Lament over Jerusalem
summary: Speaking to the crowds and his disciples, Jesus warns against the scribes and Pharisees who teach Moses' law but do not live it, and tells his followers to refuse titles and become servants. He then pronounces a series of woes on the scribes and Pharisees for hypocrisy, misplaced priorities, and the murder of the prophets, and ends with a lament over Jerusalem, whose house will be left desolate.
story: Jesus has silenced every group of questioners in the temple courts (22:46). Now he speaks about them rather than to them, in his last public teaching in Matthew. This chapter closes his public ministry: after it he leaves the temple and speaks only to his disciples, first about the temple's coming destruction (chapter 24) and then about readiness for his return (chapter 25). The woes answer the leaders' rejection of him with a prophetic verdict, and the lament at the end shows that the verdict is spoken with grief. The words about the desolate house lead straight into chapter 24, where the disciples point out the temple's buildings and Jesus says not one stone will be left on another.
historical:
The scribes were trained interpreters and teachers of the law of Moses, and many of them in Jesus' day belonged to the Pharisees, a lay movement devoted to applying the law carefully to all of life, including rules of purity and tithing, and to the traditions of earlier teachers. They were respected by ordinary people and were not the ruling elite, who were the priestly families. Their movement was the ancestor of the rabbinic Judaism that shaped Jewish life after the temple fell in AD 70. Jewish writings from later centuries also criticize hypocrites among the Pharisees, so criticism of religious show was not unique to Jesus.

Verse 35 names the first and last murders in the Hebrew Bible as it was traditionally ordered, which ends with Chronicles: Abel in Genesis 4 and Zechariah in 2 Chronicles 24:20-22, a priest stoned in the temple court for rebuking the people. Chronicles calls that Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, while Matthew says son of Berechiah, the father of the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1). Interpreters explain this as Matthew merging the two figures, as a copyist's slip, or as a reference to another Zechariah; the point, all the righteous blood from first to last, is clear on every view. Verse 14 is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is thought to have been borrowed from Mark 12:40, which is why modern Bibles omit it.
cultural:
Many details reflect daily religious practice. Moses' seat was a way of describing the authority to teach the law; some ancient synagogues had a stone seat for the teacher, though the surviving examples come from later centuries. Phylacteries were small leather boxes containing verses of Scripture, tied to the arm and forehead in obedience to Deuteronomy 6:8, and tassels were fringes on the corners of a garment commanded in Numbers 15:38-39. Making them larger turned obedience into display. The law required a tenth of the produce of the land (Deuteronomy 14:22), and some teachers extended it to kitchen herbs like mint, dill, and cumin.

Some images are vivid for their first hearers. Straining wine through cloth kept out tiny insects, which were unclean, while a camel was the largest unclean animal in the land. Tombs were whitewashed so that passersby, especially pilgrims coming to the festivals, would not touch one by accident and become ritually unclean, a practice the later Jewish law code called the Mishnah records. The white paint that warned of death is Jesus' picture of a righteous surface over an unclean heart. Gehenna, translated hell, was the name of the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a site of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), which had become a picture of final judgment.
literary: The chapter has three movements: a warning to the crowds and disciples (verses 1 to 12), seven woes addressed directly to the scribes and Pharisees (verses 13 to 36, counting without the omitted verse 14), and a lament over Jerusalem (verses 37 to 39). A woe is a prophetic form, a cry of grief and judgment together, familiar from Isaiah 5 and Habakkuk 2. Many readers notice that these seven woes mirror the Beatitudes of Matthew 5 in reverse, the teaching ministry opening with blessings and closing with woes. The images move from outside to inside: broad phylacteries, clean cups, white tombs. The speech ends not with anger but with the picture of a hen gathering her chicks, and with a quotation of Psalm 118:26, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,” which points to a future welcome.

outline.t: Do what they teach, not what they do; the greatest is a servant
Woes for shutting the kingdom and corrupting converts
Woe for neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness
Woes for outward cleanness and inward corruption
Woe for honoring the prophets and killing them

doctrines.note: Holiness is a matter of the inside before the outside. Jesus does not dismiss careful obedience, since the tithes should be kept, but he places justice, mercy, and faithfulness at the center and warns that clean surfaces can hide greed and self-indulgence.

The woes announce that the generation that rejects God's final messengers will bear the weight of all the righteous blood shed before. Judgment here is spoken by a prophet who weeps over the city he condemns.

Jesus tells his followers to refuse titles that set some above others, because they have one Teacher, one Father, and one Instructor, and are all brothers. Leadership among his people is service, and the warning applies to Christian leaders at least as sharply as to the Pharisees.

words.note: Hypokrites, hypocrite. In ordinary Greek the word meant an actor, someone who plays a part on stage behind a mask. Jesus uses it for people whose religious life is a performance for an audience, where the face shown and the heart within do not match. It is the refrain of the woes.
Ouai, woe or alas, a cry of lament used by the prophets over those facing judgment. It is not a curse but a grieving announcement of doom, and it carries sorrow as well as warning.

Geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew name of the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem. In Jesus' teaching it stands for final judgment. That he uses it of religious leaders rather than of obvious sinners is part of the chapter's shock.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus speaking with the authority of God himself. He is the one Teacher and Instructor, the Christ (verse 10). He sends prophets, wise men, and teachers (verse 34), as God sent the prophets of old. And in the lament he uses an image the Old Testament uses of God, sheltering his people under his wings (Psalm 91:4, Ruth 2:12): how often I have longed to gather your children. He grieves as Israel's God grieves over his people's refusal. The last line looks past his coming rejection to a day when Jerusalem will welcome him with the words of Psalm 118, a hope the church has read in light of his return.

hard.q: Is this chapter unfair to the Pharisees, and has it fed hostility toward Jews?
hard.a: It is a fair question, and the history is painful: Christians have used this chapter to caricature Jews and Judaism, and the word Pharisee became an insult for any hypocrite. Several points belong together. First, Jesus speaks as a Jew within Israel, in the tradition of the prophets, whose words against Israel's leaders were at least as severe (Jeremiah 7, Ezekiel 34). Second, he affirms the Pharisees' teaching of Moses' law (verse 3) and criticizes practice, not the law or the people. Third, Jewish sources themselves criticized hypocrites among the Pharisees, and many Pharisees were sincere; the New Testament names some who were sympathetic, such as Nicodemus and Gamaliel, and Paul was one. Fourth, Jesus turns the same warning on his own followers in verses 8 to 12. Read rightly, the chapter is a mirror for religious people of every kind, including Christians, and never a license for contempt.

questions: Jesus says the scribes did their deeds to be seen. Where are you tempted to practice your faith for an audience?
What would it look like in your church to take seriously the command not to seek titles and to treat the greatest as the servant?
The chapter ends with Jesus longing to gather Jerusalem like a hen gathers chicks. How does that image change the way you hear the woes before it?
